propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of IRPA of a senior immigration officer's refusal of an H&C permanent residence application.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review pursuant to subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] of the decision of a senior immigration officer wherein the application for permanent residence processed from within Canada on humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] grounds under subsection 25(1) of IRPA was refused.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of a senior immigration officer's refusal of an H&C permanent residence application under IRPA.

propositions.text: The applicant is a St. Vincent and the Grenadines citizen who came to Canada in 2003 as a visitor and has remained without status since.
propositions.quote: The applicant is a citizen of St. Vincent and the Grenadines who came to Canada in 2003 as a visitor and remained in Canada without status since that time.

propositions.text: The applicant submitted an H&C application on September 20, 2013.
propositions.quote: He submitted an H&C application on September 20, 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a St. Vincent citizen who came in 2003 and applied for H&C in 2013.

propositions.text: The applicant has sole custody of his 4-year-old Canadian citizen son with a serious permanent hearing impairment.
propositions.quote: The applicant submitted in his H&C application that he has a 4 year-old son in Canada for whom he has sole custody since his mother is unable to take care of him. His son is a Canadian citizen and has a serious and permanent hearing impairment, for which he wears hearing aids and receives care in Montréal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant has sole custody of his 4-year-old Canadian son with a serious hearing impairment.

propositions.text: If the son went to St. Vincent, he would lose medical and school services, worsening his isolation as a deaf person.
propositions.quote: If his son had to go with him to St. Vincent, he would lose the medical, therapy and school services that he benefits from as a citizen of Canada. This would exacerbate his isolation and problems as a deaf person.

propositions.text: Applicant provided medical letters confirming son's hearing impairment and need to remain in Québec for proper care.
propositions.quote: In support of this submission, the applicant provided medical letters from his son’s paediatrician and audiologist, confirming his hearing impairment. The paediatrician stated that it was in the boy’s best interests to remain in Québec, where he could receive the proper care, and the audiologist said that to her knowledge and according to the parents, adequate professional services could not be offered to him in the Caribbean.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the son would lose care if moved; applicant provided medical letters confirming son's impairment and need to stay in Québec.

propositions.text: On February 19, 2014, the officer requested information about medical care available to the son in St. Vincent.
propositions.quote: On February 19, 2014, the officer contacted the applicant requesting, among other things, information regarding the medical care available to his son in St. Vincent.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker requested information about medical care for the son in St. Vincent on February 19, 2014.

propositions.text: Applicant responded that medical care in St. Vincent is inferior to Canada, with low tech amplifiers and inferior education for deaf children.
propositions.quote: The applicant responded by letter that the medical care available to his son in Canada would not be available to him in St. Vincent. He stated that in St. Vincent, the deaf are fitted with low tech amplifiers rather than blue tooth devices that address specific needs and deaf children are given an inferior education rather than the specialized schooling and resources they receive in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant said medical care in St. Vincent is inferior to Canada for deaf children.

propositions.text: Applicant stated he attached a study from the internet explaining the bad situation for deaf children in St. Vincent.
propositions.quote: At the end of this letter, the applicant wrote: P.S. I have attached a study I found on the internet that may also help to explain the bad situation for deaf children in St. Vincent.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant said he attached a study explaining the bad situation for deaf children in St. Vincent.

propositions.text: Respondent says no such document was ever received from the applicant.
propositions.quote: However, according to the respondent, no such document was ever received.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent says no such document was ever received from the applicant.

propositions.text: On April 28, 2014, the officer refused the applicant’s H&C application.
propositions.quote: On April 28, 2014, the officer refused the applicant’s H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused the applicant's H&C application on April 28, 2014.

propositions.text: Officer found applicant provided statements but no corroborative evidence about son's medical care in St. Vincent despite request.
propositions.quote: With respect to the applicant’s son the officer stated that, despite a request for further information regarding the medical care available to him in St. Vincent, the applicant had provided additional written statements but no corroborative evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The officer found applicant gave statements but no corroborative evidence about son's medical care in St. Vincent.

propositions.text: Officer concluded son could return to St. Vincent because no evidence showed lack of resources, family could assist, and son could return to Canada anytime.
propositions.quote: The officer concluded that the applicant’s son could return with him to St. Vincent, given that: there was no evidence to suggest he would not have access to resources in St. Vincent to assist with his disability; the applicant’s family could assist with the transition period in relocating to St Vincent; and, as a Canadian citizen, he could return to Canada at any time.

paragraphs.summary: The officer concluded son could return to St. Vincent due to no evidence of lack of resources, family support, and right to return to Canada.

propositions.text: The key issue is whether the officer breached procedural fairness by not allowing applicant to provide the missing Report.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in the present case is whether the officer breached procedural fairness by failing to provide the applicant with an opportunity to provide the missing Report given that the applicant’s letter stated that it was attached.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the key issue as whether the officer breached procedural fairness by not allowing applicant to provide the missing Report.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness questions are reviewed on a correctness standard, citing Khosa, Riaji, and Galyas.
propositions.quote: A question of procedural fairness is to be reviewed on a correctness standard (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43; Riaji v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1240 at para 24; Galyas v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 250 at para 27).

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness questions are reviewed on a correctness standard, citing precedent.

propositions.text: Applicant argues officer erred by not considering or following up on the missing Report, which was relevant corroborative evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that the officer erred by failing to consider or follow-up on the report entitled “Sociolinguistic Profiles of the Deaf Communities in Trinidad, St. Vincent and Grenada” [the Report]. It was clearly relevant evidence as the officer found that, without evidence to the contrary, she was not satisfied that the applicant’s son would not have access to resources in St. Vincent to assist with his disability. The officer had a duty to request a copy of the missing study from the applicant given that it was corroborative evidence regarding the inadequacy of health services for deaf children in St. Vincent, and given that the applicant’s letter had stated clearly that the Report was “attached”.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the officer erred by not considering or requesting the missing Report, which was relevant corroborative evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent argues the Report was not submitted by applicant and should not be considered; onus is on applicant to submit evidence.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the Report, which is included in the Applicant’s Record, was not submitted by the applicant in support of his H&C application and should not be considered by the Court. The onus is on the applicant to submit the evidence in support of his application (Owusu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FCA 38 at para 8 [Owusu]; Nguyen v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 236 at paras 7-8, 13).

propositions.text: Officer gave applicant one opportunity to provide documents and had no obligation to do so again; decision was reasonable despite other evidence deficiencies.
propositions.quote: The officer gave the applicant an opportunity to provide documents once, and did not have an obligation to do so again. In any case, there were other deficiencies in the applicant’s evidence, and the officer’s decision was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Report was not submitted, onus is on applicant, officer gave one chance, and decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requires meaningful opportunity to present and have evidence considered, citing Baker, Sinnathamby, and Ghasemzadeh.
propositions.quote: Procedural fairness requires that an applicant be provided with a meaningful opportunity to present the various types of evidence relevant to his or her case and to have it fully considered (Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at para 28; Sinnathamby v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1421 at para 25; Ghasemzadeh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 716 at para 27).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent that procedural fairness requires meaningful opportunity to present and have evidence considered.

propositions.text: There is contradictory evidence about whether the Report was submitted; applicant says yes, officer says no.
propositions.quote: There is contradictory evidence in this case with respect to the Report that the applicant has included in the Applicant’s Record. The applicant affirms that the Report was submitted, while the officer affirms that it was not.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds contradictory evidence about whether the Report was submitted: applicant says yes, officer says no.

propositions.text: The Report was relevant to the officer’s best interests of the child (BIOC) analysis, as noted in the officer’s decision.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the Report was relevant to the officer’s BIOC analysis, as per this note in the decision: […] I also requested information from Mr. Miller regarding the medical care available for [his son] in Saint Vincent. In response to this request, Mr. Miller provided additional written statements. […] He further states: P.S. I have attached a study I found on the internet that may also help explain the bad situation for deaf children in St. Vincent. However to date no report has been received. Aside from Mr. Miller’s statements regarding the situation for deaf children in Saint Vincent and the lack of resources, no corroborative evidence regarding his findings has been submitted.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Report was relevant to the officer’s best interests of the child analysis, as noted in the decision.

propositions.text: The absence of the Report led the officer to find no evidence that the son would lack resources in St. Vincent.
propositions.quote: The absence of this evidence led to the following specific key finding: Without evidence to the contrary, I am not satisfied that if [his son] were to depart Canada with his father, he would not have access to resources in Saint Vincent to assist with his disability.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the absence of the Report led the officer to find no evidence son would lack resources in St. Vincent.

propositions.text: The officer should have been alert to the applicant’s statement that the Report was attached and notified him if it was missing.
propositions.quote: I agree with the respondent that while the applicant had the onus of establishing the facts on which his H&C claim rested, in the circumstances of this case the officer should have been alert to the fact that the applicant specifically mentioned in his letter that a specific document was attached, and that absent a notification from the officer, he would have no way of knowing that it was not.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the officer should have noticed the applicant said the Report was attached and notified him if missing.

propositions.text: The officer should have informed the applicant that the Report was missing and requested a copy.
propositions.quote: the officer should have informed the applicant that the Report was missing and requested a copy

propositions.text: By failing to inform the applicant, the officer breached her duty of procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: By failing to do so, the officer breached her duty of procedural fairness

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer breached procedural fairness by not informing the applicant that the Report was missing and requesting a copy.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed and the officer's decision dated April 28, 2014 is set aside.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is allowed, the decision of the officer dated April 28, 2014 is set aside

propositions.text: The matter is remitted for reconsideration by another officer.
propositions.quote: the matter is remitted for reconsideration by another officer

propositions.text: There are no questions for certification.
propositions.quote: There are no questions for certification

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the judicial review, sets aside the officer's decision, remits the matter for reconsideration, and finds no questions for certification.
